#### ! Scenario

*Or what to do when a specific version must never appear*
This scenario demonstrates rejecting a known-bad version so that resolution skips it, without forcing a downgrade that would also block future good versions.

::: {.callout-note title="Tool Versions"}
This scenario was tested with **Gradle 8.14**.
Rich version constraints (`require`/`prefer`/`strictly`/`reject`) require **Gradle 5.0+**.
Re-verified on Gradle 9.3 (October 2026): Gradle 9 raised the runtime floor to JDK 17 and changed defaults such as the configuration cache, not the resolution rules shown here.
:::

#### ! Example

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-width: 4.4
graph LR
    Root[Project Root] --> Req["lib-a: require [1.0.0, 3.0.0)"]
    Req -.-> V2["lib-a:2.0.0 (rejected)"]
    Req --> V1[lib-a:1.0.0]
```

```{.groovy include="build.gradle" snippet="s14-deps"}
```

#### ! Expect
The range `[1.0.0, 3.0.0)` resolves to the newest match, `2.0.0`, because that is what ranges do ([GS9](../scenario-9-ranges/guide.qmd)).

#### ! Actual
It resolves to `1.0.0`. The tree shows the whole request, `com.demo:lib-a:{require [1.0.0, 3.0.0); reject 2.0.0} -> 1.0.0`, and `dependencyInsight` records the reason: `rejected version 2.0.0`. Remove the `reject` line and the same build picks `2.0.0`.

#### ! Why
A rich version has several parts. `require` (or a plain version string) defines the acceptable set; `reject` removes specific versions or ranges from the candidate pool before selection. Gradle then applies its usual highest-wins choice to what remains. Rejection is therefore a *negative* constraint: it says nothing about which version to use, only which ones never to use, so a future `2.0.1` or `2.1.0` is still eligible. A `force` or `strictly` to `1.0.0` would have blocked those too.

#### ! Fix
*   **Reject the bad release** (shown above), leaving the range open for its successor.
*   **Reject a range** when a whole series is bad: `reject '[2.0, 2.1)'`.
*   **Publish the rejection in a platform** so every project in the organisation inherits it, rather than copying the line into each build.

#### ! Risk
* LOW Rejecting a single release with a known bug or CVE while the range stays open.
* MEDIUM Rejecting versions another dependency *requires*. If `lib-x` says `strictly 2.0.0` and you reject `2.0.0`, resolution fails with a conflict, which is the correct outcome but not always a welcome one.
* HIGH Using `force` to an old version instead of `reject`, and discovering a year later that the fix everyone else got was blocked by your pin.

#### ! Control
*   **Reject, don't pin,** when the goal is "not that one" rather than "exactly this one".
*   **Keep the reason with the rule:** a rejected version with a CVE number in the comment is self-explanatory; a bare `reject '2.0.0'` is not.

#### ! Check
**Fast check:** `gradle dependencyInsight --dependency lib-a --configuration compileClasspath`

**What to look for:** `com.demo:lib-a:1.0.0` selected, with the reason `Was requested: rejected version 2.0.0`; the tree line shows `{require [1.0.0, 3.0.0); reject 2.0.0} -> 1.0.0`.

**Conclusion:** `2.0.0` was removed from the candidate pool, and highest-wins chose from what was left.

#### ! Scales
Rejection is the right tool for "bad release" management at scale. A platform that rejects known-broken versions of internal libraries protects every consuming team without pinning them, and lets the next good release flow through automatically. It is also the Gradle feature closest to Python's `!=` specifier ([P4](../../python-demo/scenario-4-specifiers/guide.qmd)), which Maven can only approximate with an enforcer rule ([MS14](../../maven-demo/scenario-14-reject/guide.qmd)).

#### ! Takeaway
`reject` removes a version from the pool and lets resolution pick the best of the rest. It blocks the bad release without blocking the fix that follows it.

#### ! Wild

After Log4Shell, the useful rule was not "use 2.15.0" but "never use anything below 2.17.1", because the first two patches (2.15.0, 2.16.0) each turned out to need another. Builds that had pinned to 2.15.0 with `force` had to be edited twice more; builds that expressed the requirement as `require '[2.17.1,)'` (or rejected the vulnerable range) picked up each subsequent fix on the next resolution. The episode is the clearest argument for expressing a security policy as a rejection rather than a pin.
